coverageNote: Enumerated from disk: 7 units, 39 files — matches the expected count exactly. Units are the domain root (release-distribution-index.md, release-distribution-cx.md, 12.07, 12.08) plus the six sub-domain folders 12.01–12.06. Every file was read in full through the 3a→3b→3c cycle. Dimension scoring: 2 (Persona Specificity), 4 (Constraint Explicitness), 5 (Success Measurability) and 6 (Competitive Positioning) are marked N/A across all units — personas, constraints, success metrics and competitors are owned by meta/*.md and are referenced here, never redefined (every Role Lens and Role Matrix explicitly says so). Applicable checkpoints per unit are therefore dimensions 1, 3, 7, 8. Dimension scores below are conservative; the cross-unit contradictions found in implementer simulation are carried in the findings list rather than inflated into ❌ dimension scores, because the rubric's ❌ criteria ("major features absent", "missing MoSCoW") do not describe this tree — the specification depth is genuinely exceptional and most candidate findings were refuted on the devil's-advocate pass. 12.06 is [SURFACE] with a MoSCoW band of Could/Could/Won't, so its shallower depth is proportionate and was not penalised as a completeness failure; only its unowned expired deferral markers were scored.

findings.claim: 12.01.01 renders the readiness gate's chase items live during Draft, while 12.01.03 states the gate does not exist until validation is clean and must never be a preview — an implementer must invent whether the gate surface exists before P-1.
findings.evidence: 12.01.01-release-composition-sequencing.md:219 (States, Draft) — "**Draft** (Populated) | 1+ recordings; validation or gate unmet | Tracklist + live readiness summary split into \"your fixes\" (12.01.02) and \"waiting on people\" (12.01.03) — never one list (CX-02)." and :151-153 (Happy Path 10) — "The live readiness summary updates on every change, separating **\"you can fix this\"** (validation, 12.01.02) from **\"you are waiting on a person\"** (the gate, 12.01.03)"; :173 (edge case) — "Roll-up row: \"3 of 5 contributors aren't on WeJammin… Adding this track adds 3 people to your chase-list.\"" CONTRADICTED BY 12.01.03-delivery-readiness-gate.md:249 (States) — "Not presented | P-1 or P-3 unmet | The gate does not exist yet. User is in validation or composition. Deliberate — the gate must not be a preview of future homework." and :45-48 — "**Preconditions** are machine checks. The gate is **not presented** until they pass" and D-06 (:382) — "**Preconditions (machine) gate presentation; conditions (social) gate delivery**". P-1 is "Zero **blocking** validation findings" (:52).
findings.failure_scenario: A release in Draft has one ALL-CAPS title (blocking validation finding on Apple) and one unconsented split row. Implementer A follows 12.01.01 and renders a two-column readiness summary showing "waiting on Jamie" plus a chase-list count from the first edit. Implementer B follows 12.01.03 and renders no gate surface at all until the title is fixed. The two products differ on whether the artist can see — and per 12.01.01's "chase-list" wording, act on — contributor items before validation is clean, which is precisely the outcome 12.01.03 D-06 was written to prevent ("chasing a co-writer for a signature on a release that will be rejected for title casing spends the one favour the artist gets to ask").

findings.claim: Gate precondition P-1 is stated release-globally ("zero blocking validation findings") while validation findings are per-store by ratified decision, so a single store's blocking finding un-presents the gate and holds the whole release — contradicting 12.01.02's rule that unaffected stores stay on schedule.
findings.evidence: 12.01.03-delivery-readiness-gate.md:52 (Preconditions) — "P-1 | Zero **blocking** validation findings (warnings and advisories do not gate) | [12.01.02] | Gate not presented; user is still in validation" and :235 (edge case) — "Rule pack updates between green and dispatch | P-1 is a **precondition**, not a condition — a rule-pack regression **un-presents the gate** rather than failing it. The release falls back to validation and says why". CONTRADICTED BY 12.01.02-metadata-validation-conformance.md D-01 (:270) — "Findings are per-store scoped; no global `valid` flag" and :178 (edge case) — "**Rule pack update invalidates a gate-green release awaiting scheduled delivery** | Release falls back to **Blocked on the affected store only**; unaffected stores stay on schedule… the store is dropped from the wave and delivered late rather than delaying the release". Same shape at P-2 (12.01.03:53, "Every master analysed — pass or advisory") against 12.01.04-audio-artwork-asset-conformance.md D-04 (:255) — "Asset findings are **per-target**, never global; only a failure every selected target rejects is terminal".
findings.failure_scenario: Beatport changes a casing rule three days before a 12-store delivery. Per 12.01.02 the release falls back to Blocked on Beatport only and the other 11 stores ship on 14 Aug. Per 12.01.03's P-1, the gate is un-presented, and because conditions gate delivery, no store can be dispatched — the artist misses their announced date at 11 stores because of one store's rule. An implementer must invent whether P-1/P-2 are evaluated per store or across the release, and the two readings differ by 11 stores' worth of delivery on the artist's release date.

findings.claim: A territory-scoped rights reversion landing between gate-green and dispatch produces two opposite ratified outcomes: 12.01.03 delivers everywhere else and holds only the affected territory, while 12.02.01 blocks every partner and holds the whole release.
findings.evidence: 12.01.03-delivery-readiness-gate.md:105 (Family D, D-1) — "The delivering party's rights position was **revoked or reverted** between the recording being added and delivery (09.03.02) | **Blocking — for the affected territory only** … Territory-scoped because reversion is territory-scoped" and :233 (edge case) — "Rights revert in one territory between green and dispatch (D-1) | Territory-scoped block. **The release delivers everywhere else** | \"Your rights to track 5 reverted in Germany on {date}. We'll deliver everywhere else and hold Germany.\"" CONTRADICTED BY 12.02.01-ern-message-generation.md:114 (edge case) — "Rights change between gate-green and the delivery window (co-owner revokes; **a territory shrinks**) | Generation projects the **current** rights, finds a mismatch with the pinned scope, and blocks **all** partners rather than silently narrowing the Deal … | \"The rights on track 4 changed since you scheduled this. **We've held the whole release** rather than quietly selling it in fewer places.\"" A third position exists at 12.03.01-store-selection-territory-scoping.md D-15 (:414) — "Re-derivation at the delivery lock **halts** delivery on any change and shows a diff."
findings.failure_scenario: A co-writer's German rights revert on the Wednesday before a Friday release scheduled to 12 stores worldwide. Implementer A (following 12.01.03) delivers to all 12 stores with Germany excluded and tells the artist Germany is held. Implementer B (following 12.02.01) blocks generation for all 12 partners and the release does not come out anywhere on its announced date. Both are traceable to a ratified statement; there is no marker on either, and the artist-facing copy in the two files describes the opposite outcome as the honest one.

findings.claim: 12.04.03 D-04 ratifies "pre-saves survive a release date change" as platform behaviour, while two sibling files state the grant lives at the DSP and the guarantee may be unhonourable and must be confirmed per store before it is stated to artists — leaving the behaviour on a non-surviving store undefined.
findings.evidence: 12.04.03-pre-save-pre-add-links.md D-04 (:107) — "Pre-saves survive a release date change | A date move is not the fan's fault" and :64 (edge case) — "Release date moves | **Pre-saves must survive it** | Must hold — a date move that dropped every pre-save would be catastrophic and is not the fan's fault". CONTRADICTED BY 12.04-release-scheduling-windows-cx.md CX-05 synthesis Q1 (:80) — "The pre-save grant lives at the DSP, not with us — **we cannot re-point what we do not hold**. Whether a store's pre-save survives a date change is **the store's behaviour, not our decision**, which means D-04 in 12.04.03 ('pre-saves survive a date change') **may be an intention we cannot actually honour**. That needs confirming per store before it is stated to artists. `[PENDING — Step 5]`" and 12.04.01-release-date-lead-time.md:401-405 — "**The date-pulled-earlier case is the sub-domain's worst state-race**… the grant lives at the DSP, not with us — so 12.04.03 D-04 ('pre-saves survive a date change') may be an intention we cannot honour, per partner." The `[PENDING — Step 5]` marker carries no owner and Step 5 has completed (see moscow-ledger references throughout the tree).
findings.failure_scenario: An artist moves 14 Aug to 28 Aug with 3,400 pre-saves across Spotify and Apple. Implementer A honours D-04 literally and the UI tells the artist "your pre-saves carry" — on a store that silently drops them, 1,900 fans get nothing on 28 Aug and neither the artist nor the fan finds out (the exact silent-failure mode 12.04.03 DT-03 identifies). Implementer B treats survival as per-store profile data and shows a per-store breakdown, but no file says where that flag lives or what the fallback copy is. The domain's own "never claim more than you know" pattern is violated by whichever implementer follows D-04.

findings.claim: The Producer holds Config on 12.05.02 updates (including master replacement) and Read-only on 12.05.01 takedown, but a master replacement post-release decomposes into a takedown on several stores — so a Producer can effect a removal they have no permission to request, a hole the sub-domain CX file names and no file resolves.
findings.evidence: 12.05-catalog-lifecycle-after-release-index.md Role Matrix (:38-40) — "12.05.01 Voluntary Takedown | ✅ Full | 👁️ Read-only" and "12.05.02 Metadata Update & Redelivery | ✅ Full | ⚙️ Config". 12.05-catalog-lifecycle-after-release-cx.md CX-03 synthesis Q3 (:64) — "a Producer has `Config` on updates and `Read-only` on takedown. If their update silently decomposes into a takedown on some store, **they have effected a removal they had no permission to request. That is a real hole** and it follows directly from the shared machinery." The decomposition is ratified: 12.05.02-metadata-update-redelivery.md:61 — "*redeliver* (takedown + re-upload, losing accumulated position/streams)" and 12.01.04-audio-artwork-asset-conformance.md DT-09 (:221) — "Several DSPs will not accept an audio replacement in place at all — the real mechanism is a **takedown plus a new ISRC**", with 12.01.04 Role Lens granting the Producer that act: "Can replace a master, and sees the replacement's price before committing to it (DT-09)" (:29). No decision or open question in 12.05.01, 12.05.02 or 12.01.04 gates the Producer's update by its decomposition class.
findings.failure_scenario: A Producer fixes a mix issue on a live album and replaces the master from the DAW bridge. On Apple this decomposes into takedown + new ISRC, forfeiting stream count, playlist position and the original release date — a removal the Role Matrix says the Producer may only read about. Implementer A permits it (12.01.04 says the Producer can replace a master); Implementer B blocks it at the point of decomposition (the Role Matrix says takedown is Read-only for them). The first ships an irreversible career-scale loss executed by a party with no takedown permission; there is no marker on either statement.

findings.claim: 12.01.03 declares its condition set exhaustive, yet two sibling features route Blocking states "to the readiness gate" that no Family A–E condition covers — missing label copy and an unknown territory scope.
findings.evidence: 12.01.03-delivery-readiness-gate.md:56-57 — "**Conditions** are the gate's own: social checks over facts other humans own. **These are enumerated exhaustively below.**" Families A–E (:64-115) contain no label-copy or territory-derivation condition; the only label-copy rows are B-4/B-5, which cover a (P)-line *divergence*, not its absence. CONTRADICTED BY 12.01.05-label-copy-distributor-of-record.md States (:92) — "Empty | No ownership record in 09 | **Blocking** — routes to the readiness gate (12.01.03) rather than asking for free text here" and :82 (edge case) — "No release year available yet | (P)/(C) year cannot derive; field left empty and **flagged at the readiness gate (12.01.03)**"; and by 12.03.01-store-selection-territory-scoping.md D-07 (:406) / :71 — "**Unknown** | 09 holds no rights record for this recording, or ownership is unresolved | **Yes, but not here** — blocks and routes to the gate (12.01.03)".
findings.failure_scenario: A release reaches the gate with a complete split sheet but no derivable (P) year because the date is unset. 12.01.05 says this is Blocking and flagged at the gate; the gate's exhaustive taxonomy has no row for it, so an implementer must invent its family (which determines whether it is chaseable, whether it is overridable under Q-01, and whether it routes to a person or a case). Two implementers place it in different families and produce different affordances for the same block.

findings.claim: 12.02.03 still models `Overdue` as a first-class board state while 12.03.02 removes it from the status vocabulary and makes it a qualifier — a divergence both files flag for reconciliation that has not happened.
findings.evidence: 12.02.03-delivery-choreography-acknowledgement.md D-01 (:357) — "Silence is a first-class `overdue` **state** with an expected-response window" and its States table (:299) — "Overdue | Window exceeded, in partner business days | **`Overdue`** | \"Apple hasn't responded in {N} days\"" (the third column is explicitly "Board state (12.03.02)"). CONTRADICTED BY 12.03.02-per-store-delivery-status.md:82 — "`Overdue` is **not** a member of the vocabulary above. It is a time-in-state flag the platform raises on `Sent`, `Received` or `Accepted`" and D-19 (:393). The reconciliation is flagged twice and unresolved: 12.03.02:100-103 — "**Reconciliation note for Step 6**: 12.02.03 D-01 lists `overdue` as a first-class *state*… 12.02.03's vocabulary and this one **must be reconciled as one vocabulary during synthesis, not two**"; 12.02.03:335 — "the two state vocabularies must be reconciled into one". The same table's `Failed` and `Held` rows were updated to 12.03.02's model; the `Overdue` row was not.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer building the per-store board from 12.02.03's state table creates an `Overdue` row state, losing the `Sent · overdue` vs `Accepted · overdue` distinction that 12.03.02 DT-15 says is the only thing making the row actionable — "overdue waiting for an ack" (chase the pipe) and "overdue waiting to go live" (chase the store) collapse into one word with one escalation path.

findings.claim: 12.08 states in one paragraph that imported ISRCs are kept unconditionally and that "nothing here is pending", and in the Happy Path that they are retained "where the prefix allows" — a conditional the file defines nowhere.
findings.evidence: 12.08-catalog-migration-exit.md:36-39 — "The **ISRC half is settled**: imported ISRCs are kept **whatever prefix they came from** — 12.07 D-01 … and 12.07's migrated-catalog edge case (\"Kept, provenance = *a third party's*…\"). **Nothing here is pending.**" CONTRADICTED BY :76 (Happy Path — In, step 3) — "**ISRCs are retained where the prefix allows**; original release date is preserved in metadata where stores permit." The same line is cited as incomplete by 12.07-identifier-assignment-at-delivery.md Q-04 (:297) — "12.08 supplies no default: its Happy Path — In step 3 covers only identifiers that already exist (\"ISRCs are retained where the prefix allows\"), never their absence."
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer building catalog import reads step 3 and adds a prefix-eligibility check before retaining an imported ISRC — but no file defines which prefixes "allow" retention, so they either invent a rule (e.g. reject prior-distributor prefixes) and mint duplicate ISRCs on migrated recordings, or drop the check and contradict the Happy Path they are implementing. 12.07 D-01 ("one recording, one ISRC, forever") makes the first outcome a permanent, propagating data error.

findings.forcedInvention: What happens when an artist supplies an ISRC that WeJammin already holds for a DIFFERENT recording under the SAME rights holder — block, warn, or accept as an assertion. The implementer must invent the outcome, the affordance and whether it routes to 24.
findings.claim: 12.07's collision model covers three of four possible outcomes; the fourth — a supplied ISRC matching our own record for a different recording under the same rights holder — is unspecified, and it is the commonest real case (a paste error from the artist's own catalog).
findings.evidence: 12.07-identifier-assignment-at-delivery.md D-09 (:283) — "A supplied ISRC matching a recording we hold under a **different rights holder** is **blocked** and routed to 24 — not accepted with a warning"; edge cases (:182-184) enumerate exactly three cases: "already held here for a **different** recording **under a different rights holder**" → Blocked; "we hold for the **same** recording" → "Reuse, not collision. Silent no-op"; "belonging to a recording we do **not** hold" → "**Accepted as an assertion with a source. We cannot know.**" The Behavior section repeats the same scoping (:137-139) — "A supplied ISRC that matches a recording we already hold under a **different rights holder** is **blocked**". No row, decision or open question covers a match against a different recording held under the same rights holder, and D-14 ("Collision checking is stated as **format + our own records**") asserts we do check our own records, so the case is detected but its handling is undefined.
findings.failure_scenario: An artist pastes the ISRC of their own 2023 single into the field for a 2026 recording. The platform holds both under the same rights holder. Implementer A blocks (extending D-09's logic), Implementer B accepts it as a well-formed assertion (the case is not a 'different rights holder' hijack), producing two recordings sharing one ISRC — which 12.07 states DSPs deduplicate on, fragmenting streams, halving chart signal and splitting the royalty line permanently, with no mechanism in the standard to retract it.

findings.claim: 12.02.03 states as a correction that the delivery date must be partner lead time PLUS transfer duration; 12.04.01's ratified arithmetic and its exhaustive profile-input table omit transfer duration entirely, and no open question tracks it.
findings.evidence: 12.02.03-delivery-choreography-acknowledgement.md DT-12 (:330) — "a 12-track album at 24/96 is multi-GB **per partner**… **12.04.01's lead time must be computed as partner lead time + transfer duration**, not partner lead time alone — a store needing 10 days' notice actually needs 10 days plus however long our upload takes, and **getting that wrong misses a release date for a reason the artist can never see**. Flagged to 12.04.01 as a cross-cut rather than decided here." and :340 — "Touches **12.04.01** — trigger dependency, and **a correction**… transfer duration is the gap this file says is missing from the first." CONTRADICTED BY 12.04.01-release-date-lead-time.md §4 (:100-105) — "delivery_date(store) = release_date − lead_time(store) − rejection_headroom(store) adjusted for day_semantics(store) adjusted around blackouts(store)" — no transfer term; and §2's profile-input table (:62-70), which lists eight inputs (lead time value, day semantics, blackouts, rejection turnaround, release-time rule, non-Friday acceptance, max horizon, post-accept date change) and does not include transfer duration. 12.04.01 Q-01–Q-04 do not mention it; DT-12's flag carries no owner and no deferral target.
findings.failure_scenario: A 24-bit/96 kHz 12-track album is scheduled to 40 partners with Beatport's 10-day lead time as the binding constraint. Transfer of the derived renditions to all 40 takes 30+ hours. The scheduler dispatches at release_date − 10 days; `signal-complete` lands 1.5 days later, inside Beatport's window, and the store publishes late. The board reports honest per-store status and the artist can never trace the miss back to a scheduling formula that omitted the upload.

findings.forcedInvention: Recovery behaviour when an update that decomposes into takedown+redeliver fails between the two halves — leaving the release down and not back up. The implementer must invent whether it auto-retries, holds, alerts, or rolls forward, and what the artist is told.
findings.claim: The sub-domain CX file identifies the worst available outcome in 12.05 — a decomposing update failing halfway — and leaves its recovery on an expired `[PENDING — Step 5]` marker with no owner; neither 12.05.01 nor 12.05.02 covers it.
findings.evidence: 12.05-catalog-lifecycle-after-release-cx.md CX-03 synthesis Q1/Q2 (:62-63) — "An update that decomposes into takedown+redeliver must be atomic in intent — **a failure between the two halves leaves the release down and not back up, which is the worst outcome available in this sub-domain**." and "The second path can fail halfway. **Recovery is `[PENDING — Step 5]` and matters more than its obscurity suggests.**" Step 5 has completed (moscow-ledger.md is cited as run throughout the tree, e.g. 12.01.04 Q-02 "**RESOLVED — no. MoSCoW ran**"). 12.05.02-metadata-update-redelivery.md's edge-case table (:96-106) and States table (:111-119) contain no half-failed-decomposition row or state; 12.05.01-voluntary-takedown.md's tables do not either.
findings.failure_scenario: An artist corrects a primary-artist name on a live release. On Apple the change class resolves to redeliver; the takedown ERN is accepted and the redelivery fails conformance against a profile that moved. The release is now absent from Apple with no state describing it — 12.05.02's States offer only Updating/Updated/Partial/Rejected, none of which means "down and not back up". The implementer invents the recovery path, and the artist's record is off the largest store with no honest status.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether a claim-resolving update (attaching a clearance, adding a missed credit) is permitted while a release is suspended. The implementer must invent either a blanket block or an additive-evidence carve-out, and if a carve-out, the classifier that decides which updates qualify.
findings.claim: 12.05.02 and 12.05.03 specify a blanket update freeze during suspension, while the sub-domain CX file states the carve-out question is unresolved and records a leaning toward permitting additive evidence — leaving the platform's safety mechanism possibly blocking the resolution it waits for.
findings.evidence: 12.05.02-metadata-update-redelivery.md:102 (edge case) — "Involuntary takedown active (12.05.03) | **Updates blocked while unresolved** | \"This release is suspended. Fix the dispute first.\"" and States (:118) — "Blocked | Involuntary takedown active | Suspended, with the route to contest"; 12.05.03-involuntary-takedown-suspension.md:40-42 — "Suspension is a state on the *release*, not an event, and it **gates 12.05.01 and 12.05.02 while it lasts**." CONTRADICTED BY 12.05-catalog-lifecycle-after-release-cx.md CX-01 synthesis Q2 (:31) — "**The unresolved question is whether a claim-resolving update is exempt** (CX-04)" and CX-04 (:70, :80) — "The most interesting unresolved question in the sub-domain… CX-01 blocks exactly that. **So the platform's safety mechanism can prevent the resolution it is waiting for.** … Leaning: allow **additive evidence** (clearances, credits, attestations) during suspension; block **mutations** of the claimed facts. That distinction is worth carrying to Step 5." No open question in 12.05, 12.05.02 or 12.05.03 carries the carve-out with an owner and a live deferral target.
findings.failure_scenario: An ownership dispute is filed because a co-writer's credit was omitted. The fix is to add the credit — an additive evidence update. Under the blanket freeze the artist cannot make it and must go through 24's dispute process for a claim they concede; under the CX file's leaning they can resolve it in one action. Two implementers ship opposite behaviour for the commonest resolvable claim class, and the blanket version is the case CX-01 describes as "locked them in a room and told them the key is inside".

findings.claim: 12.04.02 leaves the behaviour of a release-date move after a pitch submission on an expired `[PENDING — Step 5]` marker with no owner, naming three mutually exclusive outcomes and choosing none.
findings.evidence: 12.04.02-editorial-pitch-windows.md:61 (edge case) — "Release date moves after pitching | **Window may reopen, close, or the pitch may be invalidated** | `[PENDING — Step 5]` — per-store behaviour unknown". Step 5 has completed (12.04.02's own Q-02 records "`/ideate-validate` ran without taking it", and sibling files record MoSCoW/Step 5 as run). The marker carries no owner and no live deferral target; Q-01 and Q-02 in the same file cover pitch APIs and pitch content, not this. The scenario is not rare: 12.04.01 D-13 explicitly permits date changes after announcement, and 12.01.01's edge-case table already specifies the adjacent focus-track case ("Focus track changed after the editorial pitch was submitted (12.04.02) | Allowed; the pitch is bound to a track and is **invalidated**").
findings.failure_scenario: An artist moves 14 Aug to 28 Aug two days after submitting their Spotify pitch. Implementer A treats the pitch as still valid (window reopened), Implementer B invalidates it and re-opens the draft, Implementer C shows it as closed. Since 12.04 CX-02 establishes the pitch window is usually the binding constraint on the date, the three behaviours differ by whether the artist retains their only editorial shot — and the file names all three without picking one.

findings.claim: 12.04.03 leaves the orphaned-pre-save case (release cancelled or taken down after fans have granted OAuth) on an expired `[PENDING — Step 5]` marker with no owner, in both its edge-case table and its States table.
findings.evidence: 12.04.03-pre-save-pre-add-links.md:65 (edge case) — "Release is cancelled or taken down | Pre-saves are orphaned; fans authorised something that will not happen | `[PENDING — Step 5]` — the permission must still be dropped" and States (:79) — "Orphaned | Release cancelled | `[PENDING — Step 5]`". The adjacent `Expired` state (:78) specifies "Fan: link resolves to the live release, never to a dead page" — which cannot apply when there is no live release. 12.05.01-voluntary-takedown.md:97 restates the gap from the other side — "Takedown during a pre-save window | Fans authorised something that will not happen | Orphaned pre-saves (12.04.03); the grant must still be dropped" — again with no owner and no deferral target. Step 5 has completed. This is the only Fan-`Full` surface in domain 12 (12.04 index Role Matrix note) and D-11 makes fans first-class users.
findings.failure_scenario: A release with 2,100 pre-saves is taken down before release day. The permission is dropped (specified), but nothing states what the fan's link resolves to, whether the fan is told, or what the artist's pre-save count now means. Implementer A resolves the link to a dead page — the exact outcome the `Expired` state forbids; Implementer B silently 404s. Either way a fan who took the one action the platform asked of them is left with no explanation, on the surface personas.md requires to be "a different product wearing the same brand".

findings.claim: 12.04.04's core content — the default milestone set and its derivation rules — sits on an expired `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` marker with no owner, while D-01 makes derivation "the whole value" of the feature.
findings.evidence: 12.04.04-rollout-plan-deadline-timeline.md:51-52 — "`[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` — **the default milestone set and its derivation rules.**" against D-01 (:109) — "Deadlines are **derived** from real lead times, windows and gate state — never templated | **The derivation is the whole value**; the task list is commodity (DT-01)". Step 5 has completed. The file's three open questions cover ownership of the tasks (Q-01, `/create-prd-architecture`), Operator visibility (Q-02, `/create-prd-security`) and the retrospective (Q-03, resolved) — none covers the milestone set or its derivation. The Overview (:10) names a milestone list in prose ("masters due, artwork due, delivered, pitch submitted, pre-save live, announce, single one, single two, release day") but no derivation rule is given for any of them except by inference from 12.04.01.
findings.failure_scenario: Two implementers build the rollout plan. A derives only the three deadlines 12.04.01 supplies (delivery date, pitch window close, gate-green-by) and treats announce/artwork/singles as artist-added soft milestones. B derives an announce milestone anchored to the first-live instant (per 12.04.01 DT-04) and an artwork deadline from asset-processing time. The two plans show different critical paths for the same release, and D-02's hard/soft rendering rule applies to different sets of items.

findings.claim: 12.02.04's field set sits on an expired `[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` marker with no owner; only the partner-adoption half is carried by a tracked open question.
findings.evidence: 12.02.04-mead-enrichment-delivery.md:41 — "`[PENDING — /ideate-discover Step 5 deepening]` — **the MEAD field set** and which partners consume it." Step 5 has completed (the same file's Q-02 records "`/ideate-discover` Step 5 ran without taking it"). Q-01 (:103) covers only "Which partners actually consume MEAD, and does it demonstrably affect placement?"; Q-02 covers correction write-back. Neither carries the field set, which drives the Role Lens split between Musician-authored descriptors ("mood, themes, what it is for") and Producer-authored ones ("tempo, key, instrumentation, whether it is live or programmed, which room it was tracked in") and therefore who is asked for what.
findings.failure_scenario: D-01 requires pre-filling from the session record and asking the Producer "only for gaps they are uniquely authoritative for". Without a field set, an implementer must invent which descriptors exist and which persona owns each — and per the Producer constraint in personas.md, asking them for one field too many means the flow is not used at all. Two implementers produce different Producer prompts from the same spec.

findings.claim: Four behavioural questions in 12.06 sit on expired `[PENDING — Step 5]` markers with no owner and no live deferral target, including whether the derived whitelist re-derives when a credit is added late.
findings.evidence: 12.06-content-id-ugc-claiming-cx.md CX-01 synthesis Q1 (:33) — "the whitelist is a projection that can go stale when a band's line-up changes or a contributor is added late (12.05.02 DT-02). **Whether it re-derives is `[PENDING — Step 5]` and matters**: a credit added post-release should plausibly whitelist that person retroactively"; CX-01 Q5 (:37) — "A contributor added to the credits *after* registration… is not on the derived whitelist and **may already have been claimed**. The two features' timelines diverge and **nothing currently reconciles them**"; CX-04 map row (:13) — "per-platform behaviour is `[PENDING — Step 5]`"; CX-05 (:14) — "whether whitelists survive withdrawal per platform is unknown". Also 12.06.01-fingerprint-registration.md:69 — "Live recording of a covered song | Same problem, harder to detect | `[PENDING — Step 5]`". Step 5 has completed; 12.06's own index Q-01 records the MoSCoW pass taking the sub-domain ("RESOLVED — the MoSCoW pass took it"). None of these markers carries an owner, and 12.06.01 Q-01/Q-02, 12.06.02 Q-01/Q-02 and 12.06.03 Q-01–Q-03 cover other questions.
findings.failure_scenario: A drummer's credit is added to a recording six months after Content ID registration (the late-credit path 12.05.02 D-02 calls the cheapest, most encouraged action). Implementer A re-derives the whitelist and retroactively releases claims against that drummer's session clips; Implementer B treats the whitelist as a one-time projection and the drummer stays claimed by a record they played on. 12.06.02 D-02's rationale — "a claim against your own drummer is not undoable socially, only technically" — is satisfied by only one of the two builds.
